instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Bank Account Fraud Alert
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, I'm calling about suspicious transactions on my account. Bank Officer: I'm sorry to hear that. I'm here to help. Can I have your account number? Customer: It's 5834-291-7465. Over the last three days, I've noticed four withdrawals totaling $1,800 that I didn't make. Officer: Let me pull that up. What are the dates of these transactions? Customer: June 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and today, June 4th. Each one is $450. Officer: I see them all here. These are ATM withdrawals, all from a machine on Bloor Street in Toronto. Are you in Toronto? Customer: No, I'm in Montreal. I haven't been to Toronto in months. Officer: That's definitely suspicious. I'm going to freeze your account immediately to prevent further unauthorized transactions. Customer: What about the money that's already been withdrawn? Officer: We'll file a fraud claim. You're not responsible for unauthorized transactions under the bank's protection policy. You should see a credit back within 5 to 7 business days. Customer: Good. What should I do next? Officer: We'll mail you a new debit card as a precaution, but don't worry about the PIN. I'm also recommending you change your online banking password right away. We'll monitor your account closely. Customer: Should I change my passwords for other accounts too? Officer: That's a wise precaution. Since someone had your card number, they might try other services. Better safe than sorry.

listeningScripts.title: Library Book Recommendation
listeningScripts.text: Emma: Have you read that mystery novel everyone's been talking about? Liam: Which one? There are so many right now. Emma: The one about the detective in Montreal. It won the Governor General's Award last year. Liam: Oh, you mean 'The Silent Case'? I haven't read it yet, but I've heard great reviews. Emma: You have to read it. I just finished it yesterday, and I couldn't put it down. Liam: Is it that good? Emma: Honestly, it's one of the best books I've read in years. The plot twists were crazy. Liam: Where did you get it? Emma: The library. I put a hold on it three months ago because everyone wanted to read it. Liam: Three months? That's a long wait. Emma: It was worth it though. If you want, I can put in a request for you. Liam: Really? That would be great. Emma: Sure. You should get it in maybe four to six weeks. Liam: Thanks. I'll add it to my reading list.

listeningScripts.title: Hospital Visitor Guidelines
listeningScripts.text: Welcome to City Hospital. We're glad you're visiting someone here. Please review our visitor guidelines for patient safety and comfort. Visiting hours are 10 AM to 8 PM daily. Each patient can have a maximum of two visitors at a time in their room. This ensures proper rest and medical care. Children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult. We restrict visits from children with colds or contagious illnesses. Visitors should wash their hands upon arrival and before leaving. Hand-sanitizer stations are located throughout the facility. Quiet voices are required in patient rooms and hallways. Please avoid using cell phones in patient areas. Photography is not permitted without the patient's written consent. Flowers and plants are welcome, but balloons are not allowed due to interference with medical equipment. Food brought from outside is permitted only if approved by nursing staff. Many patients have dietary restrictions. Visiting a patient receiving isolation care requires special precautions. Nursing staff will provide instructions. Do not disturb patients' medical equipment, monitors, or IV lines. Visitors with concerns should speak to staff at the nursing station. Parking is available in the north lot at five dollars per visit. An elevator is located near the main entrance for easy access.

listeningScripts.title: Ontario Solar Energy Initiative
listeningScripts.text: Ontario has launched an ambitious solar energy initiative targeting rooftop installations across residential and commercial properties. The program, called SolarON, aims to install solar panels on 50,000 homes and businesses over three years. The government is providing subsidies covering up to 40 percent of installation costs for eligible homeowners. Solar power currently accounts for only 1.2 percent of Ontario's electricity generation, but officials project this could increase to 8 percent by 2030. The initiative includes training programs to develop 2,500 new solar installation technicians. A rebate program offers homeowners up to 8,000 dollars toward equipment and installation expenses. Companies installing solar systems have reported a 150 percent increase in inquiries since the program's announcement. Environmental advocates praise the initiative for reducing carbon emissions and creating green jobs. The average residential system costs approximately 22,000 dollars before subsidies and rebates. Participants are also eligible for net metering, allowing them to sell excess power back to the grid.

listeningScripts.title: Local Food System Development
listeningScripts.text:
Farmer Cooperative Director Maria: We're launching an initiative to build a more resilient local food system for our region. Currently, about 87 percent of our food is imported from outside the province. We want to increase local food production and support our farmers. We're proposing a farmers market expansion and direct-to-consumer delivery programs. The cooperative will help coordinate logistics and marketing.

Grocery Store Manager Paul: I understand the value of local food, Maria, but I'm concerned about pricing and consistency. Local producers can't always compete with the prices we get from large distributors. And seasonality is an issue—in winter, local farmers have limited options. My customers expect year-round availability and competitive pricing.

Public Health Officer Dr. Sarah: Actually, Paul, local food systems have documented health benefits. Communities with stronger local food networks show 22 percent higher rates of fresh produce consumption. Plus, reducing transportation distance improves food safety and nutrition because products reach consumers fresher. And we should consider the long-term economic impact. Local spending circulates within the community.

Small Farm Owner James: I'd love to participate in this initiative. Currently, I sell about 40 percent of my production to the farmers market, but I'd like to do more direct sales. The issue is I don't have the infrastructure for packaging and distribution. If the cooperative could help with that, I could increase production by 60 percent.

listeningScripts.title: Universal Basic Income Feasibility
listeningScripts.text: I want to discuss Universal Basic Income, or UBI, and why I believe it could work in Canada. The concept is straightforward: every citizen receives a regular, unconditional cash payment from the government. Now, I know people immediately worry about the cost, but let me address that. First, UBI could replace many existing welfare programs that are expensive to administer. The bureaucracy involved in means-testing and eligibility verification costs billions. UBI would be simpler and less wasteful. Second, the economic stimulus of putting money in people's hands is significant. When people have financial security, they spend more, which supports businesses and creates jobs. Third, UBI addresses real problems: poverty, economic instability, and lack of opportunity. We've seen pilot projects in Kenya, Finland, and Canada that show positive outcomes. In Kenya, UBI increased business formation by 32 percent. In Finland, participants reported better mental health and less anxiety. Some worry it will make people lazy, but that's not supported by evidence. People want purpose and contribution, not just money. What UBI does is give them the freedom to pursue education, care for family, or start businesses without desperation. The real question isn't whether we can afford UBI—it's whether we can afford not to implement it. Rising inequality and automation are creating unprecedented challenges.
